title: Only to worship Me
hookLine: I created jinn and humans only to worship Me (51:56)
tomorrow: By the mount and the book

lines: ONE VERSE, A HANDFUL OF WORDS.
cards: Why am I here? It's the question people ask at three in the morning, or at a funeral, or in the car after a hard day. Philosophers have written libraries about it.
One answer the Qur'an gives is a single verse in Surah Adh-Dhariyat, only a handful of words in Arabic. At first it sounds almost too narrow. Then you find out what the key word holds.

teach.b: Verse fifty-six, in Pickthall's translation: "I created the jinn and humankind only that they might worship Me." The word is ya'budun, from the root '-b-d. Its noun is 'ibadah, worship.
Its other noun is 'abd, servant, as in 'Abdullah, servant of Allah. If worship means only prayer and fasting, the verse sounds like a life spent on a prayer mat. But scholars read it more widely.

teach.h: EVERYTHING ALLAH LOVES, INSIDE AND OUT.
teach.b: A classical definition, given by Ibn Taymiyyah among others, is that 'ibadah is a name for everything Allah loves and is pleased with, of words and deeds, inward and outward. That includes prayer.

It also includes honesty in a sale, kindness to parents, keeping a promise, removing something harmful from a path. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim counts that last one, moving an obstacle off a road, as charity.

Another, the first hadith in Bukhari's collection, says actions are judged by intentions. Put together, the verse widens: on this reading, almost any good act, done with the right intention, can become worship.
A report attributed to Ibn 'Abbas reads the verse as only that they might know Me, linking worship to knowing.
And verse fifty-seven adds: I seek no provision from them, nor that they feed Me. The verse says Allah doesn't need the worship; commentators say the need runs the other way.

This week: Qaf, two recorders, a gentle reminder, a block closed, the scattering winds, and a right in their wealth. They all fit here: a life where the ordinary, done with intention, becomes the purpose.

how: Muslims speak of 'ibadah as both the formal acts of worship, like prayer, fasting and zakat, and any good act done with a sincere intention; many say bismillah before ordinary tasks for this reason.

o: a monk's life spent apart from the world
the five daily prayers, and nothing more
worship: all Allah loves, in word and deed

games.q: only to worship Me — tap the pairs.
p: I seek no provision from them

s: in Islamic teaching, worship means only formal prayer
scholars define 'ibadah as everything Allah loves, of words and deeds, inward and outward.
moving an obstacle off a road is counted as charity in a hadith
it says He seeks no provision from them.

games.q: you have a pile of dishes and the verse 'only that they might worship Me' in your head. by the scholars' definition, can the dishes be worship?
o: yes, done with a good intention.
games.why: 'ibadah covers all Allah loves; with intention, ordinary work becomes worship.

practice: Think of a task waiting for you today, dishes, a report, a commute, a diaper, a phone call you've been avoiding, and picture doing it.
Now set an intention for it: carefully, for someone's good, for Allah's sake if you believe, or simply with full attention.
The task stays the same; only the intention changes, and if you pray, you can say bismillah before you start.

wordCard.voice: 'Ibadah. Worship, from the root of 'abd, servant: in 51:56, the purpose of jinn and humans, and by the scholars' definition, everything Allah loves, said or done. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: worship; from the root '-b-d, as in 'abd, servant.

carryVoice: Your line: made for worship. Worship can be wider than the prayer mat. Day five hundred ninety-five, and the week is done.
